shots.B13C093S08H04: Atri explains his name, saying he cleanses the world of sin and studies the Vedas through his nights.
shots.B13C093S08H05: Yatudhani says she cannot understand the explanation and orders him into the lake.
shots.B13C093S09H01: Vasishtha explains his name by his Yoga wealth and his life as the foremost householder.
shots.B13C093S09H02: Yatudhani says she cannot follow the explanation and tells him to plunge in.
shots.B13C093S09H03: Kasyapa explains that he guards his body and gains brightness through penance, which gives him his name.
shots.B13C093S09H04: Yatudhani again calls the explanation incomprehensible and orders him into the lake.
shots.B13C093S09H05: Bharadwaja explains that he supports his sons, pupils, deities, Brahmanas and wife, which gives him his name.
shots.B13C093S10H01: Yatudhani calls Bharadwaja's explanation incomprehensible and sends him into the lake.
shots.B13C093S10H02: Gotama says he conquered heaven and earth by self-restraint, treats all creatures alike, and was born with a light that dispelled darkness.
shots.B13C093S10H03: Yatudhani says that explanation too is incomprehensible.
shots.B13C093S10H04: Viswamitra says the gods are his friends and he is a friend to the whole universe, which is why he has that name.
shots.B13C093S10H05: Yatudhani rejects Viswamitra's explanation and orders him into the lake.
shots.B13C093S11H01: Jamadagni says he sprang from the sacrificial fire of the gods.
shots.B13C093S11H02: Jamadagni concludes that this is why he bears his name.
shots.B13C093S11H03: Yatudhani rejects this explanation and orders him into the lake.
shots.B13C093S11H04: Arundhati says she stays at her husband's side, holds the earth with him, and keeps his heart turned to her, which gives her name.
shots.B13C093S11H05: Yatudhani rejects Arundhati's explanation as well.
shots.B13C093S12H01: Ganda says her name means part of the cheek, and that she has that part a little raised.
shots.B13C093S12H02: Yatudhani rejects this explanation as incomprehensible.
shots.B13C093S12H03: Pasusakha says he protects and tends all animals and is their friend, which is why he has his name.
shots.B13C093S12H04: Yatudhani rejects this explanation and orders him into the lake.
shots.B13C093S12H05: Sunahsakha says he cannot explain his name the way the others did, and gives it to her plainly.
shots.B13C093S13H01: Yatudhani says Sunahsakha has named himself only once and she did not catch it, so he must repeat it.
shots.B13C093S13H02: Sunahsakha says that since she did not catch it, he will strike her with his triple stick and burn her to ashes.
shots.B13C093S13H03: The stick reduces the Rakshasi to ashes. The sages return from the lake to find their gathered lotus-stalks gone.
shots.B13C093S13H04: The sages ask who has stolen the stalks they gathered to eat.
shots.B13C093S13H05: The sages suspect one another and agree that each must swear to his innocence.
shots.B13C093S14H01: Atri's oath calls down penalties on the thief, such as touching cattle with his foot and studying the Vedas on forbidden days.
shots.B13C093S14H02: Vasishtha's oath lists penalties such as abandoning study, becoming an unrestrained mendicant, or selling one's daughter.
shots.B13C093S14H03: Kasyapa's oath calls down penalties such as false testimony, eating unsacrificed flesh, and sex by day.
shots.B13C093S14H04: Bharadwaja's oath lists penalties such as cruelty to women, relatives and cattle, and disrespect to one's teacher.
shots.B13C093S14H05: Jamadagni's oath lists penalties such as fouling water, having no friends, and living off a wife's earnings.
shots.B13C093S15H01: Gotama's oath calls down penalties such as throwing away the Vedas, abandoning the sacred fires, and selling Soma.
shots.B13C093S15H02: Viswamitra's oath lists penalties such as seeing his teachers supported by others, being always impure, and serving impure priests.
shots.B13C093S15H03: Arundhati's oath, phrased for a woman, calls down penalties such as humbling her mother-in-law, eating alone, and bearing a heroic son.
shots.B13C093S15H04: Ganda's oath, also phrased for a woman, lists penalties such as lying, selling her daughter, and living in slavery.
shots.B13C093S15H05: Pasusakha's oath calls down penalties such as being born of a slave-mother and having worthless children.
shots.B13C093S16H01: Sunahsakha's oath gives the thief the merit of giving his daughter to a learned Brahmana.
shots.B13C093S16H02: The sages say the oaths are no oaths at all, since all the acts listed are desirable for Brahmanas, and accuse Sunahsakha of taking their stalks.
shots.B13C093S16H03: Sunahsakha confesses that he took the stalks to test them, says he slew Yatudhani to save them, and reveals that he is Vasava, Indra.
shots.B13C093S16H04: Bhishma says the sages praise Indra and ascend to heaven with him for resisting temptation, and closes with a lesson against greed and the merit of reciting this tale.

B13C094.summary: Bhishma tells of a group of sages touring the holy waters, when Agastya finds that the lotus-stalks he gathered have been stolen. Agastya laments that righteousness is failing and says he would rather leave the world, and the sages swear their innocence with a long series of curses on the thief. Indra then confesses that he took the stalks only to hear the sages discuss duty, and he blesses the thief instead, so Agastya takes his stalks back. The chapter closes by promising merit to anyone who recites the tale.

scenes.B13C094S01: The sages, touring the holy waters, find Agastya's lotus-stalks gone. Agastya laments the decline of righteousness, and the first sages, Bhrigu, Vasishtha, Kasyapa and Gautama, swear their oaths of innocence.
scenes.B13C094S02: Angiras, Dhundhumara, Dilipa, Puru and Sukra each swear oaths of innocence and call down penalties on the thief.
scenes.B13C094S03: Jamadagni, Sivi, Yayati, Nahusha and Amvarisha each swear oaths and call down penalties on the thief.
scenes.B13C094S04: Narada, Nabhaga, Kavi, Viswamitra and Parvata each swear oaths and call down penalties on the thief.
scenes.B13C094S05: Bharadwaja, Ashtaka, Galava, Arundhati and the Valakhilyas each swear oaths and call down penalties on the thief.
scenes.B13C094S06: Sunahsakha and Surabhi swear the last oaths. Indra, pleased, blesses the thief instead of cursing him, and Agastya accuses Indra of taking the stalks.
scenes.B13C094S07: Indra says he took the stalks to hear the sages' talk of duty and asks forgiveness. Agastya takes back his stalks, and the sages go on to other holy waters, and Bhishma closes with the merit of the tale.

shots.B13C094S01H01: Bhishma tells how the sages, touring the holy waters, find Agastya's stalks gone. Agastya laments that righteousness is failing, and the sages begin their oaths of innocence.
shots.B13C094S01H02: Bhrigu's oath calls down penalties such as censuring and assailing others and eating the flesh along the backbone of sacrificed animals.
shots.B13C094S01H03: Vasishtha's oath calls down penalties such as neglecting Vedic study, leashing hounds, and living in towns as a mendicant.
shots.B13C094S01H04: Kasyapa's oath calls down penalties such as selling everything everywhere, misusing deposits, and giving false evidence.
shots.B13C094S01H05: Gautama's oath calls down penalties such as pride, subjection to desire and wrath, and farming driven by malice.
shots.B13C094S02H01: Angiras's oath calls down penalties such as impurity, Brahmanicide, and refusing expiation.
shots.B13C094S02H02: Dhundhumara's oath calls down penalties such as ingratitude to friends, birth from a Sudra woman, and eating good food alone.
shots.B13C094S02H03: Dilipa's oath calls down the misery of a Brahmana who lives in a one-well village and has sex with a Sudra woman.
shots.B13C094S02H04: Puru's oath calls down penalties such as practising medicine for money and living off his wife's and father-in-law's earnings.
shots.B13C094S02H05: Sukra's oath calls down penalties such as eating unsacrificed flesh, sex by day, and serving a king.
shots.B13C094S03H01: Jamadagni's oath calls down penalties such as studying the Vedas on forbidden days, feeding friends at Sraddhas, and eating at a Sudra's Sraddha.
shots.B13C094S03H02: Sivi's oath calls down penalties such as dying without a sacred fire, obstructing other sacrifices, and quarrelling with ascetics.
shots.B13C094S03H03: Yayati's oath calls down penalties such as sex with his wife out of season and disregard for the Vedas.
shots.B13C094S03H04: Nahusha's oath calls down penalties such as living at home after taking up mendicancy, and taking payment for teaching.
shots.B13C094S03H05: Amvarisha's oath calls down penalties such as cruelty to women, kinsmen and cattle, and Brahmanicide.
shots.B13C094S04H01: Narada's oath calls down penalties such as identifying body with soul, studying under a bad teacher, and disrespect for elders.
shots.B13C094S04H02: Nabhaga's oath calls down penalties such as lying, quarrelling with the righteous, and selling his daughter for a price.
shots.B13C094S04H03: Kavi's oath calls down penalties such as kicking a cow, urinating facing the sun, and abandoning one who seeks shelter.
shots.B13C094S04H04: Viswamitra's oath calls down penalties such as deceitful service, becoming a king's priest, and assisting at unfit sacrifices.
shots.B13C094S04H05: Parvata's oath calls down penalties such as becoming a village chief, travelling on asses, and leashing hounds for a living.
shots.B13C094S05H01: Bharadwaja's oath calls down the faults of a cruel and untruthful person.
shots.B13C094S05H02: Ashtaka's oath calls down a foolish, capricious and unrighteous rule for the thief as king.
shots.B13C094S05H03: Galava's oath calls down penalties such as being more infamous than a sinner, wronging kin, and boasting of gifts.
shots.B13C094S05H04: Arundhati's oath, phrased for a woman, calls down penalties such as speaking ill of her mother-in-law, disgust for her husband, and eating alone.
shots.B13C094S05H05: The Valakhilyas' oath calls down penalties such as begging on one foot at a village entrance and every breach of duty.
shots.B13C094S06H01: Sunahsakha's oath calls down penalties such as sleeping comfortably after neglecting the daily rite, and unrestrained conduct as a mendicant.
shots.B13C094S06H02: Surabhi's oath, phrased for a cow, calls down milking with her legs bound with human hair, by a calf not her own, into a white brass vessel.
shots.B13C094S06H03: Bhishma says that after the oaths, Indra, pleased, turns his gaze on the angry Agastya and speaks.
shots.B13C094S06H04: Indra blesses the thief instead of cursing him, granting the merit of giving a daughter to a learned Brahmana and the region of Brahman.
shots.B13C094S06H05: Agastya says Indra has uttered a blessing rather than a curse, admits that he took the stalks, and demands their return.
shots.B13C094S07H01: Indra says he took the stalks not from greed but to hear the sages discuss duty, and asks Agastya to forgive him and take them back.
shots.B13C094S07H02: Agastya takes back his stalks, the sages visit other holy waters, and Bhishma says reciting this tale on Parva days brings merit, learning and heaven.

B13C095.summary: Yudhishthira asks who began the custom of giving umbrellas and sandals at religious rites, and why. Bhishma tells how the sage Jamadagni, angry that the noon sun had delayed his wife Renuka, vowed to pierce the sun, and Surya came to him disguised as a Brahmana to argue that the sun sustains all life. The story is set up as the origin of the custom.

scenes.B13C095S01: Yudhishthira asks the origin of giving umbrellas and sandals, and Bhishma tells how Jamadagni, angry at the sun's heat, vowed to shoot it, and Surya came to plead with him.

shots.B13C095S01H01: Yudhishthira asks who introduced the custom of giving umbrellas and sandals at rites, why it was introduced, and what it means.
shots.B13C095S01H02: Bhishma introduces the tale of Jamadagni, who practises archery while his wife Renuka fetches his arrows, and she is delayed one noon by the sun's heat.
shots.B13C095S01H03: Renuka explains that the heat scorched her head and feet and she rested under a tree, and asks her husband not to be angry.
shots.B13C095S01H04: Jamadagni vows to destroy the sun with his weapons that very day.
shots.B13C095S01H05: Surya comes to him as a Brahmana and argues that he draws up water and makes rain, and so sustains food, life and every rite, asking Jamadagni to calm his anger.

B13C096.summary: Jamadagni refuses Surya's plea and insists on shooting the sun at midday, but Surya begs for protection. Jamadagni agrees to shield him and asks for a remedy against the heat, and Surya gives him an umbrella and sandals, which he declares an inflexible custom for rites. Bhishma closes by praising these gifts as meritorious in the three worlds and urges Yudhishthira to give them to Brahmanas.

scenes.B13C096S01: Jamadagni keeps his anger, and Surya, as a Brahmana, begs for protection. Jamadagni agrees to shield him and asks for a remedy for the heat.
scenes.B13C096S02: Surya gives Jamadagni an umbrella and sandals and establishes the gift as a custom. Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to give them to Brahmanas and lists the rewards.

shots.B13C096S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how Jamadagni responded to Surya's plea.
shots.B13C096S01H02: Bhishma says Jamadagni's anger does not ease, and Surya, as a Brahmana, asks how he can pierce the sun, which is always moving.
shots.B13C096S01H03: Jamadagni says he sees the sun both moving and still, and will shoot it at midday when it seems to pause.
shots.B13C096S01H04: Surya admits the offense and asks Jamadagni for protection.
shots.B13C096S01H05: Jamadagni, smiling, agrees to protect the suppliant and asks Surya to find a remedy for the heat, saying a man who slays a suppliant can commit any crime.
shots.B13C096S02H01: Jamadagni falls silent, and Surya gives him an umbrella and a pair of sandals.
shots.B13C096S02H02: Surya says the umbrella shields the head and the sandals protect the feet, and that giving them at rites will be an inflexible custom.
shots.B13C096S02H03: Bhishma says Surya began the custom, urges Yudhishthira to give umbrellas and sandals to Brahmanas, and lists the heavenly rewards for doing so.

B13C097.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for the duties of the householder and the way to prosperity. Bhishma recounts how Vasudeva asked the goddess Earth the same question. She lists the worship of Rishis, deities, Pitris and men, the daily fire rites and offerings, hospitality to guests, and food for dogs and outcasts, and says following these duties brings fame and heaven.

scenes.B13C097S01: Bhishma tells how Vasudeva asked the goddess Earth about the householder's duties, and she lists the rites of worship, offerings, hospitality and feeding others, which lead to fame and heaven.

shots.B13C097S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for all the duties of the householder and what he must do to prosper in this world.
shots.B13C097S01H02: Bhishma recounts the old tale of Vasudeva, who praises the goddess Earth and then asks her the same question.
shots.B13C097S01H03: Vasudeva asks what a householder should do, and how those acts bear good fruit.
shots.B13C097S01H04: The goddess Earth lists the duties: worship of the Rishis, deities, Pitris and men, daily fire rites, offerings to the directions, hospitality to guests, and food for dogs, outcasts and birds, all leading to heaven.
shots.B13C097S01H05: Bhishma says Vasudeva acted on this teaching, and urges Yudhishthira to do the same to gain fame and heaven.

B13C098.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the gift of light, and Bhishma recounts how Manu explained to the ascetic Suvarna why flowers and incense are offered to the deities. Sukra, teaching the Asura Vali, classifies the herbs and flowers, names the incenses each kind of being prefers, and explains that lamps give energy and are best made of ghee. The discourse ends with the Vali offerings to deities and household gods, and the teaching is handed down to Narada and then to Bhishma.

scenes.B13C098S01: Manu tells Suvarna of Sukra's teaching to Vali on flowers, incense, lamps and Vali offerings, and the teaching passes down to Narada and to Bhishma.

shots.B13C098S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what the gift of light is, how it began, and what merit it brings.
shots.B13C098S01H02: Bhishma introduces the tale of Suvarna, a learned gold-complexioned Brahmana, who meets Manu and asks why flowers are offered to the deities.
shots.B13C098S01H03: Manu introduces Sukra's discourse to the Asura Vali on the merit of flowers, incense and lamps.
shots.B13C098S01H04: Vali asks Sukra what merit flowers, incense and lamps bring.
shots.B13C098S01H05: Sukra explains the origin of herbs, sorts flowers and incenses by the beings they suit, and says lamps bring energy and are best when made with ghee; he urges Vali offerings to the deities and the household gods. He then passes the teaching down to Narada, who recounted it to Bhishma.

B13C099.summary: Yudhishthira asks why householders place their Vali offerings on the ground, and Bhishma tells how Nahusha, having won the sovereignty of heaven through merit, grew proud and made the Rishis carry his palanquin. Bhrigu comes to Agastya to complain, and Agastya explains that Brahma's boon shields Nahusha from being cursed by the Rishis. Bhrigu resolves to pull Nahusha down himself.

scenes.B13C099S01: Bhishma tells how the proud Nahusha stopped his rites and made the Rishis carry him, and how Bhrigu and Agastya discuss how to stop him, since Brahma's boon protects him.

shots.B13C099S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to repeat the merits of incense and lamps, and why householders offer Valis on the ground.
shots.B13C099S01H02: Bhishma tells how Nahusha, who won heaven by merit, kept up his rites until pride made him stop and have the Rishis carry him, and Bhrigu asks Agastya why they should endure this.
shots.B13C099S01H03: Agastya says Brahma granted Nahusha a boon that drains the power of any Rishi who sees him, so none can curse him, and he asks Bhrigu what to do.
shots.B13C099S01H04: Bhrigu says he acts at the Grandsire's command, and promises to hurl Nahusha down and curse him to become a snake, with Agastya as witness.

B13C100.summary: Yudhishthira asks how Nahusha fell from the sovereignty of the gods. Bhishma recounts how Nahusha, while pious, performed his rites, but later grew arrogant and yoked Agastya to his car. When Nahusha kicked Agastya's head, Bhrigu, who had hidden in the sage's matted hair, cursed him to become a snake, and Bhrigu then promised that Yudhishthira would one day free him. Indra was restored to heaven, and the chapter closes by urging householders to give lamps at evening.

scenes.B13C100S01: Bhishma tells how Nahusha was yoked and kicked, how Bhrigu cursed him, and how Brahma restored Indra, and closes with the merit of lamps at evening.

shots.B13C100S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how Nahusha came into distress, how he was hurled down, and how he lost the sovereignty of the gods.
shots.B13C100S01H02: Bhishma recounts Nahusha's earlier piety, his later neglect of rites, and his yoking of Agastya. Bhrigu hides in Agastya's hair, and after Nahusha kicks Agastya's head, Bhrigu curses him to become a snake, which he does; Nahusha keeps his memory and asks for the curse to end.
shots.B13C100S01H03: Bhrigu promises that a king named Yudhishthira will free Nahusha from the curse. Brahma then restores Indra to heaven, and Bhishma closes by urging householders to give lamps at evening for beauty and celestial sight.

B13C101.summary: Yudhishthira asks where those who steal or misappropriate Brahmanas' property end up. Bhishma tells of a Chandala, once a learned Brahmana, who was outcast after eating food sprinkled with milk from stolen kine, and who explains that the thieving king and everyone who drank the milk or the Soma fell into hell. A Kshatriya tells him that only giving up his life in battle to protect a Brahmana's wealth will free him, and the Chandala does so and wins a good end. Bhishma concludes that Brahmanas' property must always be guarded.

scenes.B13C101S01: Yudhishthira asks where Brahmana-property thieves go, and Bhishma introduces a Chandala and a Kshatriya, who sees the Chandala washing milk spots from his body.
scenes.B13C101S02: The Chandala explains how stolen kine's milk fell on Soma and sent the thieves and drinkers to hell, admits his own pride and sins, and asks how to be freed. The Kshatriya tells him to die in battle to protect a Brahmana's wealth, which he does, and Bhishma concludes that Brahmana property must be protected.

shots.B13C101S01H01: Yudhishthira asks where wretched men go who steal or misappropriate articles belonging to Brahmanas.
shots.B13C101S01H02: Yudhishthira's question continues, naming those who steal such articles.
shots.B13C101S01H04: Bhishma says he will recount a conversation between a Chandala and a low Kshatriya.
shots.B13C101S01H05: The Kshatriya notices the old Chandala, dust-covered and anxious about a few drops of milk on his body, and asks why he bothers to wash them off.
shots.B13C101S02H01: The Chandala tells how stolen kine's milk fell on Soma plants, sending the thieving king, his Brahmanas and all milk-drinkers to hell, and how his own pride and forbidden meat turned him from a learned Brahmana into an outcast. He asks how he may be freed.
shots.B13C101S02H02: The Kshatriya replies that only by giving up his life in battle for a Brahmana's sake will the Chandala be freed.
shots.B13C101S02H03: The Chandala gives up his life in battle to guard a Brahmana's wealth and wins a good end, and Bhishma says one should always protect Brahmanas' property.

B13C102.summary: Yudhishthira asks whether all pious men reach the same region. Bhishma tells of the sage Gautama, who raised an orphan elephant that the king Dhritarashtra, really Indra in disguise, seizes. Gautama refuses the king's gifts and follows him through each heaven the king names, until Indra reveals himself and returns the elephant. The tale ends with the promise that reciting it leads to Brahma's region.

scenes.B13C102S01: Bhishma tells how Gautama's raised elephant is seized by King Dhritarashtra, who offers wealth in its place, and Gautama refuses.
scenes.B13C102S02: Gautama vows to follow the king to Yama's realm. The king says only the faithless go there, and Gautama promises to follow him to Mandakini, the region of Kuvera.
scenes.B13C102S03: The king names the regions of the hospitable and the learned Brahmanas, and Gautama answers each with a place he will pursue him to, such as Meru's woods and Narada's woods.
scenes.B13C102S04: The king describes the regions of those who love music, are free from desire and avoid meat, and Gautama answers with the Uttara-Kuru land and Sakra's realm.
scenes.B13C102S05: Gautama and the king exchange regions for givers, Vedic students and the faithful, ranging from Soma's abode to the Sun and Varuna.
scenes.B13C102S06: The king names the regions of those who keep the Chaturmasya vow and sacrifice, and Gautama says he will follow to Indra's own abode.
scenes.B13C102S07: The king names the regions of Sakra, the Prajapatis, kings of the Rajasuya, and kine-givers and pilgrims, and Gautama answers with each.
scenes.B13C102S08: Gautama names the region of Brahma, and the king says he will not be found there. Gautama recognizes the king as Indra, who admits his identity and bows, and Gautama asks for the elephant.
scenes.B13C102S09: Indra gives the elephant back to Gautama and praises him for recognizing him. He invites Gautama and the elephant to heaven, and Bhishma closes with the merit of reciting the tale.

shots.B13C102S01H01: Yudhishthira asks whether all pious men reach the same region, or differ in status.
shots.B13C102S01H02: Bhishma says people reach different regions by their deeds, and tells how Gautama nursed an orphan elephant calf until it grew, and how Indra, disguised as King Dhritarashtra, seized it.
shots.B13C102S01H03: King Dhritarashtra offers Gautama a thousand kine, a hundred maidservants, gold and other wealth, asking what Brahmanas want with elephants.
shots.B13C102S01H04: Gautama refuses the wealth, saying Brahmanas have no use for it.
shots.B13C102S01H05: The king says elephants belong to kings, that taking this one for his vehicle is no sin, and tells Gautama to stop obstructing him.
shots.B13C102S02H01: Gautama vows to follow the king to Yama's realm and take the elephant back from him there.
shots.B13C102S02H02: The king says only the faithless and sinful go to Yama's realm, and he will go to a higher one.
shots.B13C102S02H03: Gautama says Yama's realm is where truth prevails and the weak can challenge the strong, and he will force the king there.
shots.B13C102S02H04: The king says only those who treat their own parents and eldest sister as enemies go to Yama's realm, and he will not go there.
shots.B13C102S02H05: Gautama names Kuvera's Mandakini region, where Gandharvas, Yakshas and Apsaras dwell, as the next place he will follow the king.
shots.B13C102S03H01: The king says the hospitable, the shelter-givers and those who eat what is left after feeding dependants go to Kuvera's Mandakini, and he will go higher.
shots.B13C102S03H02: Gautama names the flower-decked woods on the summit of Meru as the next place he will follow.
shots.B13C102S03H03: The king says learned, truthful and compassionate Brahmanas who make honey gifts go to such regions, and asks Gautama to name another if he knows one.
shots.B13C102S03H04: Gautama names the woods owned by Narada, filled with song, as the place he will follow the king.
shots.B13C102S03H05: The king says those who never beg and who love music and dancing go to those regions, and he will go higher.
shots.B13C102S04H01: The king says those who take delight in music and dancing and roam in joy go to such regions.
shots.B13C102S04H02: The king repeats that he will go to a higher region.
shots.B13C102S04H03: The king declares that he will not go to that region.
shots.B13C102S04H04: Gautama names the Uttara-Kuru land, where Sakra grants every wish and women live freely, as the next place he will follow.
shots.B13C102S04H05: The king says those free from desire, who abstain from meat and violence and are free from attachment, go to such regions, and he will go higher.
shots.B13C102S05H01: Gautama names the fragrant, sorrowless abode of Soma as the next place he will follow.
shots.B13C102S05H02: The king says givers who take nothing back, who are hospitable and forgiving, go to such regions, and he will go higher.
shots.B13C102S05H03: Gautama names the eternal regions at the foot of the Sun god as the next place he will follow.
shots.B13C102S05H04: The king says those devoted to the Vedas and to their teachers go to such regions, and he will go higher.
shots.B13C102S05H05: Gautama names the abode of Varuna as the next place he will follow.
shots.B13C102S06H01: The king says those who keep the Chaturmasya vow and perform a hundred and ten sacrifices go to such regions, and he will go higher.
shots.B13C102S06H02: Gautama says that above them are the regions of Indra, which are hard to reach.
shots.B13C102S06H03: Gautama says these regions are free from passion and sorrow and coveted by all men.
shots.B13C102S06H04: Gautama adds that he will follow the king even to Indra's own abode.
shots.B13C102S06H05: Gautama repeats his vow to force the king to give up the elephant.
shots.B13C102S07H01: The king says those who live a hundred years, study the Vedas and sacrifice with devotion go to Sakra's region, and he will go higher.
shots.B13C102S07H02: Gautama names the superior regions of the Prajapatis above the heavens as the place he will follow.
shots.B13C102S07H03: The king says kings who bathed after the Rajasuya and horse sacrifices go to such regions, and he will not go there.
shots.B13C102S07H04: Gautama names the eternal regions of kine, free from oppression, as the next place he will follow.
shots.B13C102S07H05: The king says those who give kine, keep celibacy and make pilgrimages to a long list of sacred waters go to the regions of kine, and he will not go there.
shots.B13C102S08H01: Gautama names the region without cold, hunger, joy or sorrow, the abode of the self-born Brahma, as the next place he will follow.
shots.B13C102S08H02: The king says those free from attachment who are devoted to Yoga and Sattwa reach Brahma's region, and Gautama will not find him there.
shots.B13C102S08H03: Gautama says he will follow the king where the Rathantara is sung and the Pundarika rite is held, and recognizes him as Indra, asking pardon for any slight.
shots.B13C102S08H04: Indra admits he is Maghavat, says he came to seize the elephant, and bows to Gautama, asking for his command.
shots.B13C102S08H05: Gautama asks Indra for the white ten-year-old elephant that he has raised as his own child.
shots.B13C102S09H01: Indra says the elephant has come to Gautama, sniffing his feet, and asks him to pray for Indra's welfare.
shots.B13C102S09H02: Gautama says he always thinks of Indra's good and asks for Indra's blessing, and he accepts the elephant as a gift.
shots.B13C102S09H03: Indra says Gautama alone among the truthful Rishis recognized him, and invites him and his elephant to heaven without delay.
shots.B13C102S09H04: Bhishma says Indra took Gautama and the elephant to heaven, and that whoever recites this tale daily reaches Brahma's region as Gautama did.

B13C103.summary: Yudhishthira asks which penance is the highest. Bhishma says fasting is the highest, and tells how King Bhagiratha reached Brahma's realm: not through his vast gifts and sacrifices, which he lists at length, but through the fast revealed by Usanas. Bhishma then urges Yudhishthira to keep the fast and to honor Brahmanas with gifts.

scenes.B13C103S01: Yudhishthira asks which penance is the highest. Bhishma answers with fasting, recounts Bhagiratha's discourse with Brahma on the great gifts that did not win heaven and the fast that did, and urges Yudhishthira to fast and honor Brahmanas.

shots.B13C103S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which penance is the highest, since Bhishma has already taught him about gifts, tranquillity, truth and compassion.
shots.B13C103S01H02: Bhishma says a person reaches the region matching his penance, and that fasting is the highest penance. He introduces Bhagiratha, who reached a region few can enter, and Brahma asks how he got there.
shots.B13C103S01H03: Bhagiratha lists his many gifts and sacrifices, saying none of them won this region, and that the fast revealed by Usanas did, which he calls the highest penance.
shots.B13C103S01H04: Bhishma says Brahma honored Bhagiratha, and urges Yudhishthira to keep the fast, honor Brahmanas with gifts, and free himself from greed.

B13C104.summary: Yudhishthira asks what makes people live long and gain fame and wealth, and whether it is penance, celibacy, recitation, medicine, deeds or speech. Bhishma answers that conduct decides all of these, and then gives a long run of daily rules. They cover rising early, prayers, cleanliness, eating, speech, sleep, sexual conduct, marriage, respect for elders and avoiding harm to others. The chapter ends by stating that conduct brings long life, fame and heaven.

scenes.B13C104S01: Yudhishthira asks what makes people live long and prosper. Bhishma answers that conduct is the key, and lists the daily rules of good conduct, ending with the praise of conduct.

shots.B13C104S01H01: Yudhishthira asks why people die young, and what brings long life, fame and wealth: penance, celibacy, recitation, medicine, deeds or speech.
shots.B13C104S01H02: Bhishma says conduct decides long life, wealth and fame, and lists a long series of daily rules: rising before dawn, prayers, cleanliness, eating, speech, sleep, sexual conduct, marriage, respect for elders and avoiding harm. He ends by saying conduct brings long life, fame and heaven.

B13C105.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat his younger brothers, and how they should treat him. Bhishma says the eldest should guide them as a good teacher guides pupils, correcting faults gently and keeping the family united. He adds that the teacher, father and mother rank in increasing reverence, and that after the father's death the eldest brother stands in his place.

scenes.B13C105S01: Bhishma explains the duties of the eldest brother toward younger brothers, including fair sharing of property, and ranks the teacher, father and mother in order of reverence.

shots.B13C105S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should behave toward his younger brothers, and how they should behave toward him.
shots.B13C105S01H02: Bhishma tells the eldest brother to treat younger brothers as a good teacher treats his pupils, correcting faults gently and not dividing the family. He ranks the teacher, father and mother in reverence, and says the eldest brother takes the father's place after his death.

B13C106.summary: Yudhishthira asks why people of every class observe fasts, and what merit and heaven the fasts bring. Bhishma repeats the teaching that Angiras gave him: Brahmanas and Kshatriyas may fast up to three nights, Vaisyas and Sudras only one, and monthly fasts bring wealth, long life and progeny. Long fasts are said to earn the merit of great sacrifices and heaven, and Angiras declares that no penance surpasses fasting, which is how the sages Viswamitra, Vasishtha and others reached heaven.

scenes.B13C106S01: Yudhishthira asks about the merits of fasting, and Bhishma repeats Angiras's rules on how long, how often and with what rewards, ending with the praise of fasting.

shots.B13C106S01H01: Yudhishthira asks why people of all classes observe fasts, what merit and heaven the fasts bring, and what to give after a fast.
shots.B13C106S01H02: Vaisampayana says that Bhishma, versed in duty, answers Yudhishthira.
shots.B13C106S01H03: Bhishma says he once asked the sage Angiras the same questions about fasting, and that Angiras answered him.
shots.B13C106S01H04: Angiras sets out the rules: Brahmanas and Kshatriyas may fast up to three nights and Vaisyas and Sudras one, and monthly fasts bring wealth, progeny and long life. Yearly and longer fasts are said to earn the merit of great sacrifices and a long stay in heaven, no fast beyond a month is prescribed, and the sages reached heaven by fasting.

B13C107.summary: Yudhishthira points out that sacrifices need wealth, so poor people cannot earn their merit, and asks for a substitute. Bhishma answers that the fasts taught by Angiras yield the same fruit as sacrifices, and then sets out a long sequence of fasts, each matched to a sacrifice and a heavenly reward. He concludes that even a poor man can reach the highest end through fasting and worship.

scenes.B13C107S01: Yudhishthira asks how poor people can earn sacrificial merit. Bhishma, citing Angiras, lists fasts of growing length, each matched to a sacrifice and a heavenly reward, and concludes that fasting gives the poor the same fruit.

shots.B13C107S01H01: Yudhishthira points out that sacrifices need wealth, and asks what rites can give poor people the same merit.
shots.B13C107S01H02: Bhishma says Angiras taught fasts that equal sacrifices, and goes through them by length and pattern, from a day or two up to a month. Each is matched to a sacrifice such as the Agnishtoma, Vajapeya or Horse-sacrifice, and to a heavenly stay, ending with Brahma's region.
shots.B13C107S01H03: Bhishma says a poor man may gain the fruit of sacrifices by fasting while also worshipping the deities and Brahmanas, and urges Yudhishthira to trust those who keep such vows.

B13C108.summary: Yudhishthira asks which sacred bathing place brings the greatest purity. Bhishma says the best is the inner Tirtha called Manasa, whose waters are truth and whose lake is understanding, and that its cleansing fruits are freedom from greed, truth, compassion and self-restraint. He adds that outer sacred places also cleanse, and that purity from both sources is the most complete.

scenes.B13C108S01: Yudhishthira asks for the greatest Tirtha. Bhishma names the inner Tirtha of Manasa, explains that inner purity surpasses water-bathing, and says outer and inner purity together are best.

shots.B13C108S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to name the foremost Tirtha, the one that brings the greatest purity.
shots.B13C108S01H02: Bhishma says the best is the inner Tirtha of Manasa, whose waters are truth and whose lake is understanding. Its fruits are freedom from greed and the virtues of truth, mildness, compassion and self-restraint, and inner purity is better than washing in water. Sacred places on earth add to this, and purity from both sources is the best.

B13C109.summary: Yudhishthira asks which fasts bring the highest and surest fruit. Bhishma gives a yearly cycle of twelfth-day fasts, each paired with worship of Krishna under a different name and the merit of a particular sacrifice. The cycle is said to culminate in the merit of all sacrifices, and the vow closes with gifts to Brahmanas, a practice that Vishnu himself declared to be unsurpassed.

scenes.B13C109S01: Bhishma recites a twelfth-day fast for each month, paired with a name of Krishna and a sacrifice's merit, and says the vow ends with gifts to Brahmanas and is unsurpassed.

shots.B13C109S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which fasts bring the highest, most beneficial and surest fruit.
shots.B13C109S01H02: Bhishma recites a fast on the twelfth day of each month, with worship of Krishna under a different name, from Kesava in Margasirsha, which earns the Horse-sacrifice, to Damodara in Kartika, which earns the merit of all sacrifices. A year of worship as Pundarikaksha brings recall of past lives, and the vow ends with gifts to Brahmanas, a fast that Vishnu declared unsurpassed.

B13C110.summary: Vaisampayana introduces Yudhishthira, who approaches Bhishma lying on his bed of arrows and asks how to gain beauty, prosperity, merit, wealth and happiness. Bhishma names the Chandravrata vow, which begins in Margasirsha when the moon stands in a set sequence of constellations matched to the parts of the body. It ends with gifts of ghee to Vedic Brahmanas and brings knowledge and fullness like the full moon.

scenes.B13C110S01: Vaisampayana introduces Yudhishthira's question to Bhishma, and Bhishma describes the Chandravrata vow, its timing by constellation and its fruit.

shots.B13C110S01H01: Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira approaches Bhishma, who lies on a bed of arrows, and puts a question to him.
shots.B13C110S01H02: Yudhishthira asks how one gains beauty, prosperity, a pleasing disposition, merit, wealth, pleasure and happiness.
shots.B13C110S01H03: Bhishma says the Chandravrata vow begins in Margasirsha, when the moon stands in a sequence of constellations matched to the parts of the body, and it ends with gifts of ghee to Vedic Brahmanas. Its fruit is knowledge and a fullness like the full moon.

B13C111.summary: Yudhishthira asks Vrihaspati what truly follows a person after death, and Vrihaspati answers that no relative goes along, only righteousness does, so one should earn wealth lawfully and live by piety. He then explains how the elements witness each deed, how the vital seed forms and how the soul enters a new body. The chapter closes with a long list of animal rebirths that follow particular sins, such as theft, betrayal, injury to teachers and parents, and adultery, and urges Yudhishthira to hold to righteousness.

scenes.B13C111S01: Vrihaspati is summoned and asked what friend follows the dead, and he answers that only righteousness follows, so one should seek lawful wealth and piety.
scenes.B13C111S02: Yudhishthira asks how piety can follow a body that becomes unseen. Vrihaspati explains that the elements and mind witness deeds, and how the vital seed forms and causes conception.
scenes.B13C111S03: Vrihaspati explains how the soul enters the seed, and then lists the animal rebirths that follow particular sins, ending with the call to hold to righteousness.

shots.B13C111S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what conduct leads to heaven or hell, and what follows a person's body into the next world.
shots.B13C111S01H02: Bhishma says Vrihaspati is coming and should be asked, since no one else can explain this mystery.
shots.B13C111S01H03: Vaisampayana says Vrihaspati arrives from the sky, is honored by all, including Dhritarashtra, and Yudhishthira puts his question to him.
shots.B13C111S01H04: Yudhishthira asks whether father, mother, son, teacher, kinsmen or friends follow the dead body, which lies like wood or clay.
shots.B13C111S01H05: Vrihaspati says each person is born, suffers and dies alone, and relatives turn away after a moment of mourning, so only righteousness follows. He urges the pursuit of righteousness and wealth won by lawful means.
shots.B13C111S02H01: Yudhishthira asks how piety can follow a body that becomes subtle and invisible.
shots.B13C111S02H02: Vrihaspati says the five elements, mind, Yama, the soul, day and night witness every deed. At death the vital breaths leave the body, and the soul takes another body.
shots.B13C111S02H03: Yudhishthira asks how the vital seed comes into being.
shots.B13C111S02H04: Vrihaspati says the elements are fed and gratified, which generates the vital seed; in union it flows and causes conception.
shots.B13C111S02H05: Yudhishthira asks how the soul grows once it enters a body.
shots.B13C111S03H01: Vrihaspati says the soul, once it enters the seed, takes a body formed from the elements, and the deities of the elements witness its deeds.
shots.B13C111S03H02: Yudhishthira asks where the soul resides, once the body and elements are gone, to feel joy and pain.
shots.B13C111S03H03: Vrihaspati explains that the soul is reborn according to its acts, that righteousness brings lasting joy, and that sinners go to Yama's realm and take lower births. He lists animal rebirths for many sins, from theft of grain, cloth, milk and oil to betrayal of trust, injury to teachers and parents, and adultery, and says the sins are exhausted in time, then urges Yudhishthira to hold to righteousness.

B13C112.summary: Yudhishthira asks what good end awaits those who have sinned. Vrihaspati answers that repentance and open confession before learned Brahmanas wash away sin, and that gifts of lawfully earned food are the greatest merit. Food is called the life of all beings, and giving it to deserving Brahmanas, according to one's own class and means, is said to free a person from hell.

scenes.B13C112S01: Vrihaspati says repentance and confession cleanse sin, and that gifts of lawfully earned food to learned Brahmanas, given by each class according to its means, are the highest merit.

shots.B13C112S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what good end sinners can reach in this world and in heaven.
shots.B13C112S01H02: Vrihaspati says repentance and confession before learned Brahmanas cleanse sin, and that gifts of lawfully earned food are the best merit, which each class may give according to its means. He stresses that food is life and that feeding deserving Brahmanas frees a person from hell.

B13C113.summary: Yudhishthira asks which of six practices, from non-injury and Vedic rites to service of teachers, brings the most merit. Vrihaspati says all six are doors to piety, but the highest good comes from universal compassion and treating all creatures as oneself, never doing to others what one would not wish done to oneself. Vaisampayana then tells that Vrihaspati rose into heaven before their eyes.

scenes.B13C113S01: Yudhishthira asks which of the six practices brings the most merit. Vrihaspati says compassion and treating others as oneself is the highest, and Vaisampayana reports that Vrihaspati ascended to heaven.

shots.B13C113S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which of non-injury, Vedic rites, meditation, self-control, penance and service to teachers brings a person the most merit.
shots.B13C113S01H02: Vrihaspati says all six are doors to piety, and that the highest good comes from universal compassion, from treating all creatures as oneself and never doing what one would not wish done to oneself. Such a person leaves no trace for others to follow, and what one does to others returns to one.
shots.B13C113S01H03: Vaisampayana says that Vrihaspati, having spoken, rose into heaven before their eyes.

B13C114.summary: Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira asks Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, how a person who has harmed others in word, thought and deed can cleanse himself of misery. Bhishma says compassion has four parts that must all be kept, and that injury arises from action, word and thought. He argues against eating meat, since its taste enslaves the mind, and recalls righteous men who gave their own flesh to save others.

scenes.B13C114S01: Yudhishthira asks how to cleanse harm done to others. Bhishma explains the four parts of compassion, the three sources of injury, and why eating meat is a sin.

shots.B13C114S01H01: Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira addresses his grandsire, who lies on the bed of arrows.
shots.B13C114S01H02: Yudhishthira says that the Rishis and deities praise compassion, and asks how someone who has harmed others in word, thought and deed can cleanse himself from misery.
shots.B13C114S01H03: Bhishma says compassion has four parts, and all must be kept, as an animal cannot stand on three legs. Injury comes through thought, word and deed, so one should first give up thought, then word, and argues against eating meat, whose taste enslaves the mind, and recalls righteous men who gave their own flesh to protect others.

B13C115.summary: Yudhishthira asks how meat offerings at Sraddhas fit with the rule against harm, and what merit or sin attaches to killing, buying and eating meat. Bhishma says abstaining from meat brings long life, strength and the goodwill of all creatures, and that the sin is shared by all who kill, buy, cook, approve or eat. He allows only meat sanctified by mantras in the Pitri rites, and closes by listing kings who abstained in Karttika and the merit of hearing this teaching.

scenes.B13C115S01: Yudhishthira asks how meat offerings square with non-injury, and Bhishma answers that abstaining from meat and harm is the highest religion, and sets out the limited cases in which meat may be used.

shots.B13C115S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how meat offerings at Sraddhas square with the rule against harm, and what merit and sin attach to killing, buying and eating meat, as well as to long life and strength.
shots.B13C115S01H02: Bhishma says abstaining from meat and harm brings long life and goodwill, and cites the views of Manu, Narada and Vrihaspati. He says all who kill, buy, cook, approve or eat meat share the sin, allows only meat sanctified by mantras in the Pitri rites, and tells of Vasu's fall for saying meat is edible. He praises abstaining in Karttika, lists the righteous kings who did so, and says hearing this teaching cleanses sin.

B13C116.summary: Yudhishthira is dismayed that people crave meat above every other food, and asks what merit comes from abstaining and what is edible. Bhishma admits that meat is tasty and strengthening, but says abstaining brings great merit, that flesh is for sacrifice, and that the slayer is in turn slain. He ends by naming abstention from cruelty as the highest religion, gift, penance and truth.

scenes.B13C116S01: Yudhishthira is dismayed at the craving for meat and asks about its merits and demerits. Bhishma admits its taste and strength, but teaches that abstaining from cruelty is the highest virtue.

shots.B13C116S01H01: Yudhishthira is dismayed that people crave flesh above all other foods, and asks Bhishma about the merit of abstaining and what is edible.
shots.B13C116S01H02: Bhishma agrees that meat is tasty and strengthening, but says abstaining brings great merit, that flesh is for sacrifice, and that one who kills is in turn killed. He calls abstention from cruelty the highest religion, gift, penance, truth and friendship.

B13C117.summary: Yudhishthira asks what fate awaits those who die in battle, whether they wish to die or live. Bhishma tells of Vyasa, who came upon a worm fleeing a passing cart, and asked why it was so afraid. The worm replies that every creature clings to life, and reveals that it was once a cruel Sudra usurer whose memory survives through a single act of honoring a Brahmana guest.

scenes.B13C117S01: Yudhishthira asks about those who die in battle. Bhishma tells how Vyasa met a worm fleeing a cart, and the worm explains its fear of death.
scenes.B13C117S02: The worm explains why it clings to life, recalls its cruel life as a Sudra usurer, and asks Vyasa what is good for it.

shots.B13C117S01H01: Yudhishthira asks why many die in battle, whether desiring death or life, and what end they reach, since giving up life is hard.
shots.B13C117S01H02: Bhishma says all creatures live by their own nature, and tells the old tale of the sage Vyasa, who saw a worm moving fast on a road where carts passed.
shots.B13C117S01H03: Vyasa asks the worm why it is in such haste and what it is fleeing.
shots.B13C117S01H04: The worm says the rumble of a large cart and the bulls' breathing terrify it, and that death is painful and life hard to win, so it flees from happiness into woe.
shots.B13C117S01H05: Vyasa tells the worm that, as a lowly creature without the pleasures of the senses, death might be a benefit to it.
shots.B13C117S02H01: The worm says every creature clings to the state it is in, so it wants to live. It recalls that it was a cruel Sudra usurer who neglected guests and the gods, but that it once honored a Brahmana guest, which kept its memory, and it asks Vyasa for guidance.

B13C118.summary: Vyasa tells the worm that its memory survives because of one good deed and that it may rise again through merit. The worm stays on the road, is crushed by the cart, and after many animal births is reborn a Kshatriya through Vyasa's grace. Vyasa reminds him of his past sin and says that dying bravely in battle for kine or Brahmanas will lift him, step by step, toward the status of a Brahmana.

scenes.B13C118S01: Vyasa says the worm can rise again through merit. The worm is crushed by the cart and reborn a Kshatriya, thanks Vyasa, and Vyasa explains the steps by which a low birth can rise.

shots.B13C118S01H01: Vyasa says the worm's memory survives through a past merit, and that it may rise again; the worm stays on the road, is crushed by the cart, and after many animal forms is reborn a Kshatriya, coming back to thank Vyasa.
shots.B13C118S01H02: The reborn Kshatriya describes his princely fortune, thanks Vyasa, and asks what he should now do.
shots.B13C118S01H03: Vyasa praises the Kshatriya's gratitude, notes his old sin, and says he may rise to a Brahmana by dying bravely in battle for kine or Brahmanas, since lower births rise by steps through Sudra, Vaisya and Kshatriya.

B13C119.summary: The reborn Kshatriya, recalling his earlier births, undertakes severe austerities, and Vyasa tells him that protecting all creatures is the penance of his order. He rules his subjects righteously, becomes a Brahmana, and Vyasa consoles him that only the loss of righteousness, not death, is to be feared. The former worm then reaches Brahma's realm, and Bhishma says the Kshatriyas who fell at Kurukshetra also attained a good end, so Yudhishthira should not mourn them.

scenes.B13C119S01: The Kshatriya, recalling his past births, undertakes penance, and Vyasa tells him to protect his subjects. He becomes a Brahmana, and Vyasa consoles him about death.
scenes.B13C119S02: The former worm sets up a thousand sacrificial stakes and reaches Brahma's realm, and Bhishma tells Yudhishthira not to mourn the Kshatriyas who fell at Kurukshetra.

shots.B13C119S01H01: The reborn Kshatriya, remembering his previous births, begins severe austerities, and Vyasa comes to see him.
shots.B13C119S01H02: Vyasa says a Kshatriya's penance is the protection of all creatures, and that by keeping to it he will become a Brahmana.
shots.B13C119S01H03: The Kshatriya, though living in the woods, rules his subjects righteously and, after casting off his Kshatriya body, becomes a Brahmana. Vyasa comes to him again.
shots.B13C119S01H04: Vyasa tells him not to fear death, since righteous acts bring good births, and that only the loss of righteousness should be feared.
shots.B13C119S01H05: The former worm, now a Brahmana, thanks Vyasa for lifting him from happiness to greater happiness through righteousness.
shots.B13C119S02H01: The former worm sets up a thousand sacrificial stakes and reaches Brahma's realm. Bhishma says the Kshatriyas who fell at Kurukshetra also attained good ends, and urges Yudhishthira not to mourn them.

B13C120.summary: Yudhishthira asks which is superior, knowledge, penance or gifts. Bhishma tells how Vyasa, travelling in disguise, was fed by the sage Maitreya at Varanasi and laughed in delight, and Maitreya asked why. Vyasa explains that gifts surpass ablutions and sacrifices, names non-injury, truth and giving as the three best vows, and urges Yudhishthira to give freely and rejoice.

scenes.B13C120S01: Yudhishthira asks which is superior. Bhishma tells of Vyasa's meeting with Maitreya, and Vyasa explains that gift is the highest sacred act and the three tracks of conduct.

shots.B13C120S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which is superior among knowledge, penance and gifts.
shots.B13C120S01H02: Bhishma tells how Vyasa, in disguise, was fed by the sage Maitreya at Varanasi and laughed aloud in delight, and how Maitreya asked why.
shots.B13C120S01H03: Vyasa explains that gifts surpass ablutions and Vedic vows, names non-injury, truth and giving as the three tracks of the best vow, and notes that people are righteous, sinful or neither. He urges Yudhishthira to give, sacrifice and rejoice.

B13C121.summary: Maitreya, a learned sage of a wealthy line, replies to Vyasa's teaching on gifts. He praises Vyasa's purity, and argues that learned, pure-born Brahmanas are the field in which gifts bear fruit. A gift to an unworthy receiver ruins both giver and taker, while the merit of a gift to a worthy one is shared equally.

scenes.B13C121S01: Maitreya praises Vyasa, and argues that gifts bear fruit only when made to learned, pure Brahmanas, and that worthy receivers share the giver's merit.

shots.B13C121S01H01: Bhishma says Maitreya, a learned sage of a prosperous line who valued righteous acts, answers Vyasa's words.
shots.B13C121S01H02: Maitreya says Vyasa is right, and asks permission to speak.
shots.B13C121S01H03: Vyasa invites Maitreya to say whatever he wishes.
shots.B13C121S01H04: Maitreya praises Vyasa's teaching and purity, and argues that Brahmanas who have penance, Vedic learning and pure birth are the field of gifts, and that gifts to unworthy receivers are wasted and harm both sides. Gifts to the worthy bring merit to giver and receiver alike, and such Brahmanas deserve worship.

B13C122.summary: Vyasa replies that penance is greater than gifts, since it destroys sins and wins the Vedas and heaven, though gifts and learning are also praised. He advises Maitreya on the duties of a householder, including contentment between husband and wife. He then blesses Maitreya and departs, and Maitreya returns the blessing.

scenes.B13C122S01: Vyasa answers that penance surpasses gifts, advises Maitreya on householder duties, and leaves with a blessing that Maitreya returns.

shots.B13C122S01H01: Vyasa praises Maitreya's knowledge and says penance surpasses gifts, since it cleanses sins and wins the Vedas and heaven, while gifts also bring happiness and honour, and the worthy deserve respect. He advises Maitreya on householder duties, blesses him, and departs; Maitreya returns the blessing.

B13C123.summary: Yudhishthira asks how good and faithful women behave. Bhishma tells of the heavenly woman Sumana, who asks Sandili how she reached heaven, and Sandili answers that she did not win it through outward signs, but through devoted service to husband, in-laws, guests and gods, with careful and discreet household conduct. Bhishma adds that reading this tale at full and new moons leads to heaven.

scenes.B13C123S01: Bhishma tells how Sandili, asked by Sumana how she reached heaven, describes her devotion to her husband and household, and says reading this tale brings heaven.

shots.B13C123S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe the conduct of good and chaste women.
shots.B13C123S01H02: Bhishma tells how Sumana asks Sandili how she reached heaven. Sandili answers that outward signs are not what won it, but her devotion to her husband, in-laws, guests and gods, her discretion, honesty, and careful household conduct.
shots.B13C123S01H03: Bhishma says Sandili departs after speaking, and that anyone who reads this story at full and new moon gains heaven and great joy.

B13C124.summary: Yudhishthira asks whether conciliation or gifts is more effective. Bhishma tells how a Brahmana seized by a Rakshasa stayed calm and used conciliation, asking why the Rakshasa was so pale and lean. The Brahmana then flattered him with a long list of reasons, each a kindly account of his troubles, and the pleased Rakshasa made him a friend, gave him wealth and let him go.

scenes.B13C124S01: Yudhishthira asks whether conciliation or gifts is more effective. Bhishma tells how a Brahmana, seized by a Rakshasa, appeased him with flattery and won his release.

shots.B13C124S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which is more effective, conciliation or gifts.
shots.B13C124S01H02: Bhishma says people are moved by conciliation or gifts according to their nature, and tells how a calm Brahmana, seized by a Rakshasa, asked why the Rakshasa was so pale and lean.
shots.B13C124S01H03: The Brahmana gives a long list of flattering reasons for the Rakshasa's paleness, each sympathetic to his troubles. The Rakshasa, pleased, makes him a friend, gives him wealth and lets him go.

B13C125.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a poor man should act, and which gift is best and when. Bhishma prefaces his answer with the mysteries of duty taught by Vyasa, then recounts a heavenly messenger's question to the Pitris about the three rice-balls of the Sraddha and the ban on sexual relations on Sraddha days. The chapter continues with rites of purification, the sins against the sun, wind, fire and cows, and gifts such as blue bulls, sesame and lamps that free a man from his debt to his ancestors.

scenes.B13C125S01: Yudhishthira asks how a poor man should act and which gift is best. Bhishma begins the teaching, and a heavenly messenger asks the Pitris about the three rice-balls of the Sraddha and the ban on sex on Sraddha days.
scenes.B13C125S02: The Pitris explain the fate of each rice-ball, and the sage Vidyutprabha asks Indra how to atone for killing lesser creatures. Indra and Vrihaspati give rites of purification and list the sins against the sun, wind, fire and cows, and the gods ask the Pitris how to repay the debt to ancestors.
scenes.B13C125S03: The Pitris explain the merit of freeing blue bulls, giving sesame and water on the new moon, and lighting lamps in the rains, and Bhishma closes the teaching.

shots.B13C125S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a poor man should behave, which gift is best, and when each should be given.
shots.B13C125S01H02: Vaisampayana says that Bhishma, thus questioned by the king, begins to explain these mysteries of duty.
shots.B13C125S01H03: Bhishma says these mysteries come from Vyasa and from Yama's penance, and lists the beings they please and the people to whom gifts should not be made. A heavenly messenger then asks the Pitris why sex and feasting are barred on Sraddha days, and about the three rice-balls.
shots.B13C125S01H04: The Pitris say that a man who has sex or eats at a Sraddha on that day lies in his seed for a month. They direct that the first rice-ball go into water, the second be given to the wife, and the third be cast into fire.
shots.B13C125S01H05: The messenger asks what each of the three rice-balls reaches, and how each one gratifies the deities and rescues the Pitris.
shots.B13C125S02H01: The Pitris praise the question and say only Markandeya fully knows these rites. The first ball gratifies the moon, the wife's ball brings children, the fire ball grants wishes, and the officiating Brahmana must keep purity that day.
shots.B13C125S02H02: Bhishma says the sage Vidyutprabha asks Indra how men can atone for killing worms, ants, snakes and birds.
shots.B13C125S02H03: Indra prescribes bathing at holy places for three days and touching a cow's back. Vidyutprabha adds a rite of eating Shashtika rice with milk, and standing on one foot on a mountain facing a fire, which cleanses sins.
shots.B13C125S02H04: Vrihaspati names sins such as urinating facing the sun, disrespect for the wind, neglect of the fire and milking cows whose calves are very young, and lists their harms. The gods then ask the Pitris which acts please them and how to repay the debt owed to them.
shots.B13C125S02H05: The Pitris answer that freeing blue bulls, giving sesame and water on the new moon, and lighting lamps in the rains clear that debt, and that begetting children rescues ancestors from hell. Gargya asks what merits these gifts bring.
shots.B13C125S03H01: The Pitris say that a freed blue bull's water and mud satisfy the ancestors for long ages, lamps in the rains bring radiance, and sesame-and-water gifts at the new moon bring healthy children. Bhishma closes by saying he has explained everything in order.

B13C126.summary: Indra asks Vishnu what acts please him, and Vishnu says that honoring Brahmanas, hospitality, and worship of the Aswattha tree and the cow are his favored worship. Baladeva, the deities, Dharma, Agni and Viswamitra then give rules on sacred vessels, the unfit recipients of Sraddha offerings, the sin of kicking cows, fire or Brahmanas, and a prayer to the cow. The chapter closes with Brahma's answer to the seven Rishis: drinking moonlight after a bath on the Pausha full moon under Rohini earns the merit of great sacrifices, for those who lack wealth.

scenes.B13C126S01: Indra asks Vishnu what pleases him. Vishnu says honoring Brahmanas and worshipping the Aswattha and the cow please him most, and Baladeva adds a dawn rite of touching cow products and mustard seeds.
scenes.B13C126S02: The deities, Dharma, Agni and Viswamitra give rules on copper vessels, unfit Sraddha recipients, the sin of kicking a cow, fire or Brahmana, a Bhadrapada rite and a prayer to the cow.
scenes.B13C126S03: The seven Rishis, led by Vasishtha, ask Brahma how the poor can earn sacrificial merit, and Brahma gives the moonlight rite of Pausha.

shots.B13C126S01H01: Bhishma says Indra asks Vishnu what acts gratify him, and how men can please him.
shots.B13C126S01H02: Vishnu says that detracting Brahmanas displeases him, and that worshipping Brahmanas, honoring guests, and worshipping the cow, the Aswattha and cow-dung whirl all count as worship of him.
shots.B13C126S01H03: Indra asks why Vishnu praises such small things, since Vishnu creates and destroys all things.
shots.B13C126S01H04: Vishnu smiles, recalls his victories as the boar, the dwarf and the disc, and says that feeding Brahmanas and dawn worship bring the merit of purity and the blessing of Amrita.
shots.B13C126S01H05: Baladeva says that touching a cow, ghee, curds, mustard and Priyangu at dawn cleanses sin, and that the Rishis avoid impurity during Sraddhas.
shots.B13C126S02H01: The deities say that using a copper vessel with water for vows and offerings makes a devotee's wishes succeed, while the same acts done otherwise bring little merit.
shots.B13C126S02H02: Dharma says Sraddha offerings must not go to Brahmanas who serve kings, keep cattle, trade, act, quarrel or marry Sudra women, and that a guest sent away hungry brings loss on the host.
shots.B13C126S02H03: Agni says the man who kicks a cow, a Brahmana or a blazing fire faces infamy, lasting hell, and rejection of his offerings, so one should never touch them with the feet.
shots.B13C126S02H04: Viswamitra says that offering rice boiled in sugared milk at noon in Bhadrapada under Magha, facing south in an elephant's shade, earns Sraddha merit for thirteen years.
shots.B13C126S02H05: The cow gives a prayer to be said while adoring her, which cleanses sins and wins the region of Indra.
shots.B13C126S03H01: Vasishtha and the seven Rishis circle Brahma and ask how men of good conduct, without worldly means, can gain the merit of sacrifices.
shots.B13C126S03H02: Brahma says that on the Pausha full moon under Rohini, bathing and lying under the open sky, then drinking the moon's rays, earns the merit of great sacrifices.

B13C127.summary: A run of short teachings, each given by a different sage or deity, on ritual conduct: offerings on lunar days, household objects and habits that drive away the gods and ancestors, and rules of hospitality. The last teaching, from Jamadagni, says a pure heart counts for more than costly sacrifice. The section treats ritual merit as depending on both correct practice and inner purity.

scenes.B13C127S01: A string of teachings from Vibhavasu, Sree, Angiras, Gargya and Dhaumya on offerings, the household items that displease the gods, and the duties that bring merit.
scenes.B13C127S02: Jamadagni teaches that an impure heart undoes even great sacrifices, while a pure heart is worth as much as them.

shots.B13C127S01H01: Vibhavasu (Surya) describes two offerings to the sun on full-moon days and warns that cutting trees or using a tooth-stick on new-moon days brings sin and angers the ancestors.
shots.B13C127S01H02: Sree says a house with scattered vessels and beaten women drives the gods and ancestors away, so they refuse its offerings.
shots.B13C127S01H03: Angiras says a man's offspring multiply if he stands under a Karanja tree every night for a year with a lamp and Suvarchala roots in his hand.
shots.B13C127S01H04: Gargya lists duties such as hospitality, lamps at sacrifice halls, no daytime sleep, no meat, and no harm to cows and Brahmanas, and says the gods reject Sraddha offerings when impure women are near.
shots.B13C127S01H05: Dhaumya says broken pots and beds, roosters, dogs and trees growing inside the house are inauspicious, so no tree should be planted at home.
shots.B13C127S02H01: Jamadagni says a man with an impure heart goes to hell even after grand sacrifices, and a poor Brahmana's small gift of barley with a pure heart earned him Brahman's realm.

B13C128.summary: Vayu gives duties for the four rainy months and for ancestral rites, and names faults that bring sin, such as letting a Sudra kindle the sacred fire or letting unqualified women take part in rites. He gives an expiation of three days of fasting and fire offerings made with a mixture of cow's urine, dung, milk and ghee. He ends by saying that those who avoid these faults or expiate them reach heaven.

scenes.B13C128S01: Vayu's rainy-season duties, the sins of improper ritual helpers, and the three-day expiation that restores the sinner's standing.

shots.B13C128S01H01: Vayu lists rainy-season offerings to the ancestors and Brahmanas, names sins such as letting a Sudra light the fire or letting unfit women assist, gives a three-day expiation, and promises heaven to those who avoid or cleanse these faults.

B13C129.summary: Lomasa warns that men who seek other men's wives, have intercourse with barren women, or take what belongs to a Brahmana are cut off by their ancestors, and their offerings fail. He then praises gifts of ghee, Akshata, sesame-filled vessels, water, lamps and Krisara food on lunar days. He says these gifts earn great merit from the gods and ancestors, and that gifts of cows, land or an Agnishtoma sacrifice count as equal merit.

scenes.B13C129S01: Lomasa's warnings against adultery, barren women and theft from Brahmanas, followed by praise of gifts such as sesame vessels and lamps and the merit they bring.

shots.B13C129S01H01: Lomasa warns against adultery, sex with barren women and taking Brahmana property, then praises gifts of ghee, sesame, water, lamps and Krisara food and says what merit each brings.

B13C130.summary: The sages ask Arundhati, wife of Vasishtha, to reveal a high mystery of duty. She says it should be taught only to faithful or pure-hearted listeners, and describes washing a cow's horns and letting the water fall on one's head as bathing in all sacred waters. Brahman, Yama and Surya then speak in turn, praising gifts of water, lamps, Kapila cows, sandals and umbrellas and naming five kinds of sinners to avoid.

scenes.B13C130S01: Arundhati's teaching on the cow-horn rite, the praise of the gods, and the words of Brahman, Yama and Surya on charitable gifts and the five sinners to shun.

shots.B13C130S01H01: Bhishma says the sages ask Arundhati, wife of Vasishtha, to disclose a high mystery of duty.
shots.B13C130S01H02: Arundhati says the teaching should reach only faithful or pure-hearted listeners and describes the cow-horn rite; the gods and sages applaud her.
shots.B13C130S01H03: Brahman praises her teaching and grants that her penances will keep growing.
shots.B13C130S01H04: Yama relays Chitragupta's teachings on water, lamps, sandals, umbrellas and Kapila cows, and Surya then names five kinds of sinners to avoid.

B13C131.summary: The gods, ancestors and sages ask the Pramathas, night-wandering spirits, why they harm some men and what stops them. The Pramathas list unclean acts that leave men open to attack, such as neglecting purification after intercourse, insulting elders and spitting into water. They also name protections for a home, such as sacred marks, Akshata grain, a fire that never goes out, and certain animal skins, animals or sacrificial smoke.

scenes.B13C131S01: The Pramathas explain which conduct makes men vulnerable to them and which household practices keep them away.

shots.B13C131S01H01: Bhishma says the gods, ancestors and sages ask the Pramathas why they afflict some men and what acts protect against them.
shots.B13C131S01H02: The Pramathas name the unclean acts that make men easy prey and then list the protective marks, offerings, fires and household objects that keep them out.

B13C132.summary: Brahman sends the naga Renuka to ask the eight elephants that hold up the world about the mysteries of duty. The elephants prescribe Vali offerings of treacle and rice at an ant-hill on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in Karttika, saying the rite gives merit and eases their burden of holding up the earth. The gods, ancestors and sages applaud Renuka.

scenes.B13C132S01: Brahman sends Renuka to the elephants, who teach an ant-hill offering that brings merit and supports their work of holding up the earth.

shots.B13C132S01H01: Bhishma says the Grandsire Brahman names the naga Renuka and sends him to the mighty elephants that hold up the world.
shots.B13C132S01H02: Renuka asks the elephants to teach him the mysteries of religion and duty.
shots.B13C132S01H03: The elephants prescribe Vali offerings at an ant-hill with mantras, flowers, sugar, rice and cloth, describe their rewards, and the gods and sages applaud Renuka.

B13C133.summary: Maheswara closes this run of teachings by praising cows. He says feeding cows each day for a month while eating one meal a day brings great merit, and he notes the bull on his standard as a sign of his favour for them. Even one day's feeding of cows, he says, gives a fourth part of the merit of a person's good deeds in life, so cows should be worshipped by all.

scenes.B13C133S01: Maheswara teaches that feeding and worshipping cows brings great merit, and explains why he favours them.

shots.B13C133S01H01: Maheswara says a month of daily feeding of cows, with one meal a day for oneself, brings great merit, and mentions the bull on his standard as a sign of his favour for cows.

B13C134.summary: Skanda and Vishnu each teach a further duty and promise great rewards for hearing, reciting or performing it. Bhishma then says this knowledge is worth more than the whole earth. He adds that it must be withheld from the faithless, atheists, the unkind, and those who see other creatures as separate from themselves.

scenes.B13C134S01: Skanda's earth-and-honey rites, Vishnu's praise of hearing and reciting these teachings, and Bhishma's warning about whom to teach.

shots.B13C134S01H01: Skanda teaches two rites: smearing the body with earth from a blue bull's horns and bathing after three days, and offering honeyed food in a copper vessel to the full moon.
shots.B13C134S01H02: Vishnu says that daily hearing, reading or reciting these teachings keeps a person from evil and fear and brings merit.
shots.B13C134S01H03: Bhishma calls this knowledge more precious than the whole earth and says it must not be taught to the faithless, atheists, the unkind, and others he names.

B13C135.summary: Yudhishthira asks from whom each of the four classes may accept food. Bhishma says Brahmanas may eat with Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaisyas but never accept food from a Sudra, and he sets out the rules for the other classes. He names sources that defile, such as physicians, harlots and mechanics, and lists givers whose food must be refused, including killers of cows or Brahmanas and drunkards.

scenes.B13C135S01: Yudhishthira's question on eating rules, and Bhishma's answer on whose food each class may accept and whose it must refuse.

shots.B13C135S01H01: Yudhishthira asks from whom a Brahmana may accept food.
shots.B13C135S01H02: He adds the same question for a Kshatriya, a Vaisya and a Sudra.
shots.B13C135S01H03: He completes the question about the Vaisya and the Sudra.
shots.B13C135S01H04: Bhishma sets out which givers each class may take food from, and says that food from Sudras, physicians, harlots and others is defiling, while the duties of each class are briefly described.

B13C136.summary: Yudhishthira asks what expiation a Brahmana must make after accepting various foods and gifts, especially those used for the gods and ancestors. Bhishma gives a long list of purification rites, each tied to the kind of food or gift and the setting, such as funerals, eclipses and a dead person's house. He ends by saying that eating food partly eaten by another class is cleansed by smearing the body with auspicious substances.

scenes.B13C136S01: Yudhishthira's question about expiations, and Bhishma's list of purification rites for different foods, gifts and settings.

shots.B13C136S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what expiation a Brahmana must perform after accepting different foods, especially those offered to the gods and ancestors.
shots.B13C136S01H02: Bhishma lists expiations for accepting many foods and gifts and for eating in a dead person's house or with other classes, and ends with a rite for food partly eaten by another class.

B13C137.summary: Yudhishthira asks whether charity or devotion is the greater merit. Bhishma answers with a list of kings and sages who reached heaven through their gifts, teaching or penance, such as Sivi, Pratardana and Rantideva. He says their fame will last and that he will answer further doubts in the morning, as night has come.

scenes.B13C137S01: Yudhishthira asks which is better, charity or devotion, and Bhishma lists the royal and sage donors who gained heaven, then defers further answers to morning.

shots.B13C137S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which is better in this world, charity or devotion.
shots.B13C137S01H02: Bhishma names kings and sages, from Atreya and Sivi to Bhagiratha, who reached heaven through gifts, teaching or sacrifice, says their fame lasts, and promises to answer more questions in the morning.

B13C138.summary: Yudhishthira asks how many kinds of gift there are, what each brings, and to whom each should be given. Bhishma answers that gifts are made for five motives: a wish for merit, a wish for profit, fear, free choice, and pity. He gives an example for each and says gifts raise the giver's merit and fame, and that Brahman advised giving according to one's power.

scenes.B13C138S01: Yudhishthira's questions about kinds of gift, and Bhishma's classification of gifts by motive.

shots.B13C138S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how many kinds of gift there are, what fruits each brings, and to whom each should be made.
shots.B13C138S01H02: Bhishma names five motives for giving, illustrates each with a short example, and says gifts increase merit and fame.

B13C139.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to teach on religion and profit, and Bhishma agrees to tell of Vishnu's power and a doubt that troubled Rudra and his spouse. He describes how Krishna, during a long vow, received sages at his hermitage, where fire from his mouth burned a mountain and then was called back and the mountain restored. When the sages ask about it, Krishna says the fire is his own energy and asks them to tell him something wonderful, and they choose Narada to recount a story.

scenes.B13C139S01: Yudhishthira's request, Bhishma's opening, and Krishna's vow-time episode in which fire from his mouth burns and then restores a mountain, followed by his explanation to the sages.
scenes.B13C139S02: The ascetics ask Narada to tell the story of the Himavat wonder, and he begins.

shots.B13C139S01H01: Yudhishthira praises Bhishma's learning and asks him to teach on religion and profit, since no one else can now serve as their teacher.
shots.B13C139S01H02: The narrator, Vaisampayana, says Bhishma, moved by affection for the king, prepares to answer.
shots.B13C139S01H03: Bhishma promises tales of Vishnu's power and of a doubt that troubled Rudra and his spouse, and describes Krishna's long vow, when sages came and a fire from his mouth burned a mountain and was then restored.
shots.B13C139S01H04: The sages praise Krishna as creator and destroyer and ask him to explain the fire.
shots.B13C139S01H05: Krishna says the fire is his own energy from a penance for a son equal to him, and asks the sages to tell him something wonderful they have heard.
shots.B13C139S02H01: The sages ask Narada to relate the wonder they saw on the Himavat mountains, and he begins his story.

B13C140.summary: Narada tells of Shiva (Mahadeva) resting on the Himavat mountains, surrounded by gods, ghostly beings and sages. Uma playfully covers his eyes, plunging the world into darkness, and a third eye then opens on his forehead and burns the mountain until Shiva restores it at her plea. Uma asks why he has the third eye, why he burned and restored the mountain, and why his faces, hair and throat look as they do. Shiva agrees to explain.

scenes.B13C140S01: Narada describes Shiva's retreat on the Himavat, Uma covering his eyes, the third eye that burns the mountain, and Uma's questions about his form and actions.
scenes.B13C140S02: Shiva is pleased and agrees to explain the reasons for his forms.

shots.B13C140S01H01: Bhishma introduces Narada's account of a discourse between Sankara and his spouse Uma.
shots.B13C140S01H02: Narada describes Shiva seated on the Himavat among gods, ghosts and sages, then Uma covering his eyes, the third eye opening and burning the mountain, and Shiva restoring it at her plea.
shots.B13C140S01H03: Uma asks why the third eye appeared, why he burned the mountain, and why he then restored it.
shots.B13C140S01H04: Shiva answers that her covering of his eyes plunged the world into darkness, so he made the third eye to protect creatures, and he later restored Himavat to please her.
shots.B13C140S01H05: Uma asks why his faces differ, why his hair and throat are as they are, why he always holds the Pinaka, and why he is a Brahmacharin, and says she wishes to share his duties.
